section_summary: This section documents mounting American public, congressional, commercial, and administrative debate over exports of petroleum, scrap iron, aircraft materials, nickel, and other strategic commodities to Japan during its war in China. It includes antiwar petitions and constituent correspondence demanding an embargo, petroleum-import and Canadian metals statistics, internal State Department discussions of the moral embargo, and correspondence from oil companies and aircraft-industry representatives. The papers repeatedly note that a comprehensive embargo required new legislation while examining whether existing moral and export controls were effective.

subfiles.title: Petition against American support for the Japanese invasion of China—Cunningham copy
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Urges the United States to end exports that assist Japan's war in China.
subfiles.summary: The petition condemns Japan's invasion, aerial bombing, and violations of the Nine-Power Treaty and Kellogg Pact. It argues that American scrap iron, oil, aircraft, trucks, and other materials make the United States complicit in destruction in China.

subfiles.title: Petition against American support for the Japanese invasion of China—Methodist copy
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Calls for practical measures to halt American trade supporting Japanese aggression.
subfiles.summary: This copy repeats the appeal to end American exports useful to Japan's military campaign. The handwritten endorsement and church identification are largely illegible in the OCR.

subfiles.title: Petition against American support for the Japanese invasion of China—Jensen copy
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Demands an end to American shipments that facilitate Japan's attack on China.
subfiles.summary: The signer associates Japanese aggression with the bombing of civilians and destruction of foreign institutions in China. The petition asks for direct or indirect action against the supply of oil, scrap, aircraft, and other materials.

subfiles.title: Petition against American support for the Japanese invasion of China—Abraham copy
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Requests action to stop American materials from sustaining Japan's war.
subfiles.summary: This signed copy repeats the argument that American commerce is aiding violations of international treaties and the destruction of Chinese civilians. The signer appears to be associated with Calvary Baptist Church in Alexandria.

subfiles.title: Petition against American support for the Japanese invasion of China—unsigned copy
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Seeks termination of American trade contributing to Japanese aggression in China.
subfiles.summary: The page contains the full standard petition but no legible signature. It invokes peace, international law, the Good Neighbor principle, and the protection of Chinese civilians.

subfiles.title: Petition against American support for the Japanese invasion of China—Issugu copy
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Calls for an end to exports of American strategic materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The petition protests the use of American aircraft, shells, petroleum, trucks, and scrap iron in Japan's war. The handwritten signature and address are poorly recognized by the OCR.

subfiles.title: Petition against American support for the Japanese invasion of China—Church of Our Saviour copy
subfiles.from: Unidentified member of the Church of Our Saviour, Brookland Parish
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Asks the federal government to stop trade aiding Japan's invasion.
subfiles.summary: This church-associated copy reproduces the standard antiwar petition. It condemns profiteering from Japanese aggression and requests every practicable means of ending the trade.

subfiles.title: Petition against American support for the Japanese invasion of China—Grace Church copy
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Opposes American commercial participation in Japan's war against China.
subfiles.summary: The petition repeats the charge that American raw materials and weapons sustain Japanese military operations. The handwritten endorsement appears to identify a Grace Church affiliation, but much of it is illegible.

subfiles.title: Petition against American support for the Japanese invasion of China—Gould copy
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Urges action to end supplies that enable Japan to attack China.
subfiles.summary: The standard petition is signed by a person associated with Francis Asbury Methodist Church in Washington. It emphasizes civilian suffering and American responsibility for exports of strategic goods.

subfiles.title: Petition against American support for the Japanese invasion of China—Methodist Washington copy
subfiles.from: Unidentified Methodist petitioner in Washington, D.C.
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Requests measures to terminate American trade sustaining the Japanese war effort.
subfiles.summary: This copy contains the standard petition and an illegible handwritten church address. It denounces Japanese aggression and American sales of oil, scrap, aircraft, shells, and trucks.

subfiles.title: Petition against American support for the Japanese invasion of China—Bagwell copy
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Calls for an end to American exports assisting Japanese aggression.
subfiles.summary: The signer is identified with Francis Asbury Methodist Church in Washington, D.C. The petition argues that continued strategic trade makes Americans partners in the destruction of China.

subfiles.title: Petition against American support for the Japanese invasion of China—E. C. Bu copy
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Opposes the export of American materials used in Japan's invasion of China.
subfiles.summary: This signed copy repeats the standard demand for direct or indirect action against the trade. The signer's surname and address are incomplete in the OCR.

subfiles.title: Petition against American support for the Japanese invasion of China—addressed copy
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Demands that American commerce cease supporting Japan's war.
subfiles.summary: The page contains the standard petition and an illegible address notation. It presents the export trade as complicity in Japanese aggression and civilian destruction.

subfiles.title: Petition against American support for the Japanese invasion of China—unsigned copy
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Requests an end to strategic exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The final petition copy in this group is unsigned or has no legible signature. It repeats the appeal based on peace, treaty obligations, and protection of Chinese civilians.

subfiles.title: Roger S. Greene transmits oil-company correspondence
subfiles.about: Forwards three oil-company letters concerning petroleum sales to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Greene sends replies from the Atlantic Refining Company, Texas Pacific Coal and Oil Company, and Pure Oil Company. He argues that their positions suggest substantial petroleum-industry support for a voluntary or compulsory embargo against Japan.

subfiles.title: Atlantic Refining Company denies supplying Japan
subfiles.about: States that Atlantic Refining is not supplying oil or gasoline to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Rollins replies to Potter's inquiry of April 13. His brief response unequivocally denies that the company supplies Japan with oil or gasoline.

subfiles.title: Texas Pacific discusses sources of Japanese petroleum imports
subfiles.about: Suggests that Japanese gasoline and oil imports chiefly come from Pacific Coast refiners.
subfiles.summary: Penn says he lacks definite information on the issue. He nevertheless believes that gasoline and oil exported from the United States to Japan originate principally with Pacific Coast refiners and marketers.

subfiles.title: Pure Oil Company denies supplying Japan
subfiles.about: Says Pure Oil cannot identify exporters to Japan but is not itself supplying them.
subfiles.summary: Dawes cannot tell Potter which American companies supply Japanese gasoline and oil purchases. He states clearly that Pure Oil is not among them.

subfiles.title: State Department acknowledgment of Greene's oil-company letters
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges and notes the three petroleum-company replies forwarded by Greene.
subfiles.summary: Yost reports that the Division of Controls has read the letters from Atlantic Refining, Texas Pacific, and Pure Oil. He thanks Greene for providing the material without making a policy commitment.

subfiles.title: Telegram to Tokyo on the Secretary's moral-embargo remarks
subfiles.about: Reports the Secretary of State's press response concerning Japan and aviation-gasoline equipment.
subfiles.summary: The telegram describes a question about an alleged Japanese protest against extending the moral embargo to aviation-gasoline manufacturing plans. It distinguishes national-defense conservation restrictions from moral restrictions on commodities used to bomb civilians.

subfiles.title: Press-conference exchange on the moral embargo
subfiles.about: Records the Secretary's answer about a reported Japanese protest over aviation-gasoline restrictions.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary says he has not verified the reported protest. He explains that some exports are restricted for defense conservation and others under a moral embargo directed against aerial attacks on civilians.

subfiles.title: Memorandum and tables of Japanese and Manchurian petroleum imports, 1937–1939
subfiles.about: Transmits privately compiled statistics on petroleum-product imports into Japan and Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Moseley says P. L. Hopper obtained the figures from Standard-Vacuum Oil Company field employees and considers them reasonably reliable because Japan had not published comparable data. The attached tables break down petroleum imports by origin and product for Japan and Manchukuo during 1937–1939, including gasoline, kerosene, diesel and fuel oil, lubricants, wax, and asphalt. Hopper intended also to supply the data to naval and military intelligence.

subfiles.title: Duplicate memorandum on Japanese and Manchurian petroleum statistics
subfiles.about: Duplicates the covering memorandum explaining the source and value of the petroleum tables.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum attributes the figures to Standard-Vacuum personnel in the field and says they cover most petroleum imports into Japan and Manchuria. It notes their intelligence value and Hopper's plan to share them with military agencies.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Charles Rist on French and Canadian nickel policy
subfiles.about: Records Rist's report that France and Canada would not release nickel for Japanese purchase.
subfiles.summary: Grady gave Rist an oral response based on Herbert Feis's March 28 memorandum concerning the Franco-Japanese treaty. Rist confidentially stated that French domestic requirements prevented nickel sales to Japan and that Canada had reached the same decision.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs comments on the proposed reply to France
subfiles.to: Office of the Adviser on International Economic Affairs
subfiles.about: Suggests correcting the proposed reply and considering a parallel statement to Canada.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern Affairs notes Canada's importance as a nickel supplier to Japan and recalls the Canadian minister's discussions with Hickerson. It asks whether Canada should receive guidance similar to that proposed for France, while recognizing that only France had formally asked.

subfiles.title: Routing note on the proposed nickel-policy formula
subfiles.from: Office of the Adviser on International Economic Affairs
subfiles.about: Requests approval of a formula before submitting it to the Secretary of State.
subfiles.summary: The short note asks whether the proposed response is satisfactory. If accepted, it is to be submitted to the Secretary for approval.

subfiles.title: Suggested oral reply to Charles Rist on nickel sales to Japan
subfiles.from: Office of the Adviser on International Economic Affairs
subfiles.about: Proposes telling France how nickel sales might undermine the American moral embargo.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum explains that molybdenum is covered by the moral embargo and that nickel can substitute for it in aircraft manufacture. Although the choice belongs to France, the draft suggests that France consider the effect on American policy, interests, and public opinion. A notation indicates the formula was approved by the Secretary.

subfiles.title: Grady asks Feis to obtain the Secretary's decision
subfiles.about: Asks Feis to check the nickel issue with the Secretary and advise Professor Rist.
subfiles.summary: Grady reports that he was unable to see the Secretary that evening. He asks Feis to obtain a decision on the marked question and communicate it to Rist.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Charles Rist on wartime economic problems
subfiles.about: Records Rist's inquiries about wartime trade, tungsten purchases, and French nickel sales to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Rist discussed suspected war-material shipments through Vladivostok and neutral countries surrounding Germany, as well as French tungsten procurement. He also asked whether the United States objected to France selling Japan enough nickel for its domestic needs under a renewed treaty. Grady promised to seek information and consult colleagues.

subfiles.title: Notes respecting exports of non-ferrous metals from Canada
subfiles.about: Corrects press claims and explains Canadian controls on nickel, copper, aluminum, lead, and zinc exports.
subfiles.summary: The notes deny that Canadian producers had recently sold nickel to the Soviet Union and detail the rejection of Soviet orders and restrictions on Japanese purchases. They describe prewar contracts with Mitsui, refused Japanese requests, and export-permit controls after September 1939. Further sections explain continuing copper shipments, reduced aluminum exports, and contrasting lead and zinc sales to Japan.

subfiles.title: “U. S. Metal Trades Squeezed by Allies”
subfiles.about: Argues that the moral embargo injured American metal producers without depriving Japan, Germany, or the Soviet Union of substitutes.
subfiles.summary: Keller claims that restrictions on American molybdenum allowed British and French nickel and Chinese tungsten to replace it in foreign munitions production. He argues that Japan and the Soviet Union had accumulated reserves and could obtain substitutes while American producers lost markets. The article characterizes the policy as strategically ineffective and economically harmful.

subfiles.title: Statement of Canadian non-ferrous-metal exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Tabulates Canadian exports of copper, nickel, aluminum, lead, and zinc to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The table compares September figures for 1938 and 1939 with five-month totals ending in February 1939 and 1940. It provides quantities in hundredweights for several forms of strategic non-ferrous metals.

subfiles.title: Senator Wiley forwards Haseltine's embargo letter
subfiles.about: Forwards a constituent's objections to shipments of scrap iron and gasoline to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Wiley asks the State Department to review W. E. Haseltine's letter and return it. He also requests whatever comment the Secretary wishes to make on the constituent's argument.

subfiles.title: W. E. Haseltine advocates a complete trade embargo
subfiles.about: Calls for legislation prohibiting trade with Japan because of aggression and treaty violations.
subfiles.summary: Haseltine argues that scrap iron, gasoline, and other American goods are helping Japan become a political, economic, and military threat. He says local opinion strongly supports prompt and drastic action and recommends banning trade with any country that breaks a treaty with the United States.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Senator Wiley
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Haseltine's letter and encloses the Department's direct reply to him.
subfiles.summary: Welles thanks Wiley for forwarding the constituent correspondence. He returns Haseltine's letter and supplies a copy of the Department's response.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to W. E. Haseltine
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains that no existing statute authorizes the comprehensive embargo Haseltine proposed.
subfiles.summary: Yost acknowledges Haseltine's views on shipments of scrap iron, gasoline, and other materials to Japan. He states that a general embargo would require new legislation.

subfiles.title: Congressional memorandum forwarding Williamson's letter
subfiles.about: Forwards a constituent letter about scrap-iron exports for departmental information.
subfiles.summary: The brief House memorandum says the attached letter concerns a subject of interest to the recipient. It transmits the document without additional policy comment.

subfiles.title: Maurice R. Williamson requests an end to scrap-iron exports
subfiles.about: Asks Congress to stop exporting scrap iron to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Williamson argues that ending a small segment of American export trade might stop the war in China and prevent a future conflict with the United States. He asks Schaefer to support immediate legislation.

subfiles.title: State Department acknowledgment to Representative Schaefer
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of Williamson's letter concerning scrap-iron shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Welles thanks Schaefer for sending the constituent letter for the Department's information. The response makes no substantive commitment concerning an embargo.

subfiles.title: Telephone memorandum arranging a China-aid delegation meeting
subfiles.about: Requests an appointment for eight to ten representatives of the Washington Committee for Aid to China.
subfiles.summary: Wheeler proposes several times on May 29 or May 31 for the delegation's visit. A notation selects 3:30 p.m. on Wednesday, May 29.
keywords: Washington Committee for Aid to China

subfiles.title: Initial appointment note for Graves's joint delegation
subfiles.about: Seeks a meeting for delegates from two organizations opposing aid to Japanese aggression.
subfiles.summary: Wheeler requests an appointment on behalf of Mortimer Graves for six or eight representatives. The proposed delegation includes members of both the Washington Committee for Aid to China and the American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression.

subfiles.title: Washington Committee for Aid to China transmits a peace-rally resolution
subfiles.about: Forwards a resolution passed by approximately 800 people at an April 5 peace rally.
subfiles.summary: Graves calls Hamilton's attention to a resolution unanimously adopted at the National Press Club Auditorium. The committee reports attendance of about 800 Washington citizens.
keywords: Washington Committee for Aid to China

subfiles.title: Peace-rally resolution demanding an embargo on war materials
subfiles.from: Peace Rally at the National Press Club Auditorium
subfiles.about: Demands immediate legislation ending shipments of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The resolution says American permission for such shipments encourages Japanese aggression in China. It asserts that public opinion favors China and faults Congress for nearly three years of inaction.

subfiles.title: Hamilton acknowledges the peace-rally resolution
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the committee's resolution concerning war-material shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton says the Department has carefully noted the resolution passed at the April 5 rally. He thanks Graves for bringing it to the Department's attention.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to report on Japanese attempts to obtain Bolivian ores
subfiles.about: Points to a despatch reporting Japanese efforts to acquire larger supplies of tin and other ores from Bolivia.
subfiles.summary: The sheet states that Japan was desperately seeking greater and continuing ore supplies. It also reports efforts to persuade Bolivia to buy arms in exchange for metals if a workable arrangement could be devised.

subfiles.title: Eyslop criticizes State Department policy toward aggressor states
subfiles.about: Challenges the Department to justify its limited moral-embargo policy toward Japan and other aggressors.
subfiles.summary: Eyslop argues that critical examinations of policy receive no weight because they conflict with the views of Hull and his staff. He encloses a newspaper column and asks how officials rationalize a policy that leaves only voluntary restraint between American war traders and aggressor governments.

subfiles.title: “I'd Rather Be Right” column on American scrap exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Argues that American scrap metal and oil are building the Japanese naval and military threat.
subfiles.summary: Grafton contrasts the cost of selling scrap to Japan with the much larger expense of constructing American battleships to meet the resulting danger. He contends that American supplies sustain Japan's conquest of China and rejects the claim that an embargo would itself create the danger of war.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck replies to Eyslop's criticism
subfiles.about: Defends policymaking as an integration of many official and public views.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck directs Eyslop back to the final paragraph of his April 18 letter. He rejects the suggestion that policy is determined by one or two officials and emphasizes the role of many people, including the general public.

subfiles.title: Barrington requests Japanese export statistics
subfiles.about: Requests figures for exports of gasoline, scrap iron, oils, and machine tools to Japan and asks what is being done to stop them.
subfiles.summary: Barrington seeks values for the listed commodities during 1939 and 1940 to date. He describes the exports as destructively used against the Chinese and requests a report on the Department's record.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to E. S. Barrington
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Refers Barrington's statistical inquiry to Commerce and explains the lack of statutory embargo authority.
subfiles.summary: Yost says the Department of Commerce maintains the requested export data and will reply directly. He adds that a general embargo on war materials to Japan would require new legislation.

subfiles.title: William Ives requests Japanese export statistics from the State Department
subfiles.about: Requests data on strategic exports to Japan and an account of efforts to stop them.
subfiles.summary: Ives asks for 1939 and current 1940 values of gasoline, scrap iron, fuel oil, lubricating oil, and machine tools sent to Japan. He characterizes these materials as being used destructively against China.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to William Ives
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Refers Ives's request to Commerce and states that new legislation would be needed for an embargo.
subfiles.summary: Yost explains that the Department of Commerce keeps the relevant statistics and will answer Ives directly. He repeats that no statute authorizes the proposed embargo on war materials to Japan.

subfiles.title: State Department transmittal to the Secretary of Commerce
subfiles.about: Transmits the Barrington and Ives letters for statistical replies.
subfiles.summary: The State Department sends copies of both Huntington correspondents' requests concerning the value of exports to Japan. Copies of the Department's replies to the two men are enclosed for context.

subfiles.title: William Ives requests Japanese export statistics from the President
subfiles.about: Sends the White House the same request for export figures and action against strategic shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Ives lists gasoline, scrap iron, fuel oil, lubricating oil, and machine tools and asks for 1939 and 1940 export values. He also asks what the administration is doing to prevent their use against China.

subfiles.title: State Department acknowledgment of the White House referral
subfiles.from: Department of State, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the White House referral and directs Ives to the Department's earlier reply.
subfiles.summary: The Department confirms receipt, through the White House, of Ives's April 30 inquiry. It refers him to its May 3 response to his identical letter sent directly to the State Department.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck endorsement of Hiss's memorandum
subfiles.about: Endorses Mr. Hiss's view and recommends bringing his memorandum to the Secretary.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck states that he shares the position expressed by Hiss. He recommends submitting the underlying memorandum to the Secretary; the following page contains only illegible routing material.

subfiles.title: Chamber of Commerce Export Department transmittal note
subfiles.about: Forwards or comments on a memorandum concerning export policy and supporting statistics.
subfiles.summary: Taylor's handwritten note is badly degraded in the OCR but appears to discuss an attached export-related memorandum and its distribution. He indicates that his bureau is approaching the problem and has assembled supporting annual statistics.

subfiles.title: “The Moral Embargo” aircraft-industry position paper
subfiles.about: Criticizes the selective moral embargo on aviation goods as ineffective and economically damaging.
subfiles.summary: The paper accepts the condemnation of civilian bombing but argues that restrictions aimed chiefly at aircraft manufacturers impose costs without stopping Japan's war in China. It contends that petroleum, scrap metals, machine tools, and indistinguishable raw materials continue to sustain Japanese military and aircraft production, while the embargo redirects business to foreign competitors. It proposes lifting the aeronautical restraint, imposing a comprehensive trade ban, or permitting exports of demonstrably commercial aircraft.

subfiles.title: Greene forwards Senator Austin's view of an embargo
subfiles.about: Transmits Warren Austin's cautiously favorable response to a proposed embargo on war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Greene emphasizes Austin's influential position within the Senate minority. He notes that the senator appears sympathetic to an embargo but refuses to make an advance commitment.

subfiles.title: Senator Warren Austin responds to the non-participation committee
subfiles.about: Expresses a natural inclination toward the embargo proposal while reserving freedom of decision.
subfiles.summary: Austin credits the factual statements in “Shall America Stop Arming Japan” because of his confidence in the committee's personnel. He says he is disposed to favor an embargo but will not commit himself before the Senate considers the subject.
